title: Array positions
summary: Find items by their numbered places in an array. Update one score, check a safe index, and compare the same task in six languages.
introduction: Picture three numbered lockers holding scores. If you know the locker number, you can go straight to it. Arrays use the same idea, but their first position is numbered zero.
learningObjectives: Read and update an array item by index
Find the last valid position from the length
Check a position before reading it

blocks.text: An **array** keeps items in order. An **index** is an item's position number. Index 0 means the first item, index 1 the second, and index 2 the third.
The **length** is the number of items. Three items have length 3, but their valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2. The last index is length minus 1.

A fixed-size array cannot grow in place. C, Java, and this C# example use fixed-size arrays. JavaScript arrays and Python lists can grow. We keep the length fixed in every example to practise the same task.

items: Start with scores 4, 7, and 2 at indexes 0, 1, and 2.
Choose index 1. Check that it is at least 0 and less than the length 3.
Replace the score at index 1 with 9. The array is now 4, 9, 2.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

variants.caption: Run this JavaScript in the browser playground, or save main.js and use Node.js.
Use a separate local C11 compiler. Save this complete program as main.c; see Language setup.
Use a separate local C++17 compiler. Save this complete program as main.cpp; see Language setup.

variants.code:
scores = [4, 7, 2]
index = 1
if 0 <= index < len(scores):
    scores[index] = 9
    print(scores[index])

blocks.text: Square brackets pick a position. The line with = stores a new value in that position. It replaces 7; it does not add another item. Reading or replacing a known array position takes O(1) work.
Check the small and tricky cases
An empty array has no valid index. The same check rejects every index when length is 0. The C example uses a real three-item array; do not write a zero-length C array to test emptiness.

Out-of-range behavior differs. Java and C# report an error. JavaScript can give undefined. C and C++ can access memory they should not. Python allows some negative indexes. Our check accepts only the shared range 0 through length minus 1.
Inserting into the middle is different from replacing an item. In an array-backed list, insertion can require shifting many later items and take O(n) work.

items: Change index from 1 to 2. Keep the replacement value 9.
The program still prints 9, but now the array becomes 4, 7, 9. The final item changed instead of the middle one.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not use index <= length as the upper check. Index length is already one place too far. Use index < length.
